h1: The 7 Best Ergonomic Keyboards Under $100 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: seven ergonomic keyboards under $100, from split and wave designs to a keyboard and mouse combo, with clear budget picks.
summary: The Perixx PERIBOARD-512B is the best ergonomic keyboard under $100, a genuine fixed-angle split with a padded wrist rest in the $25 to $50 bucket. The Logitech Wave Keys is the easiest to adapt to. The two Arteck splits cover wireless and backlit needs, and the ProtoArc adds a matched mouse.
intro: A budget ergonomic keyboard fails in two predictable ways: the layout is only curved for show, or it is so different from a flat board that you give up inside a week. Under $100 you can avoid both by deciding what kind of ergonomics you want before you look at prices. A gentle curve and a true split fix different problems.

We reviewed seven keyboards on paper, all in the $25 to $50 or $50 to $100 price buckets, comparing layout, wrist support, connection and extras. A budget RGB gaming keyboard in this data was left out because it is not an ergonomic design. The most useful split in this ranking is not price but how much your hands must relearn.

products.name: Perixx PERIBOARD-512B Wired Ergonomic Keyboard - Split Keyboard with Wrist Rest
products.verdict: The cheapest genuine split layout with a padded wrist rest.
products.description:
The PERIBOARD-512B is a wired split keyboard with a fixed angle and a padded wrist rest, in the $25 to $50 bucket. A true split separates the two halves so your forearms sit closer to straight, which is the point of ergonomic design. It also drops the battery and pairing, because it simply plugs in.

It tops the list because a genuine split at this price is rare. The Arteck splits cost a full bucket more, and the Logitech Wave Keys is a one-piece wave, which is a milder correction. What you accept is a fixed angle and a cable, the two things the wireless Arteck and Logitech avoid.

Buy it for the lowest cost route to a split design. The caveat is adjustment: a fixed angle cannot be tuned to your shoulder width, and the layout takes days to learn.
products.idealFor: Shoppers who want a split design for the least money.
products.skipIf: You want wireless or an adjustable angle.

products.name: Logitech Wave Keys Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard - Graphite
products.verdict: A one-piece wave with a cushioned palm rest and little learning curve.
products.description:
The Logitech Wave Keys uses a one-piece wave-shaped frame with a cushioned attached palm rest and wireless connection, in the $50 to $100 bucket. The wave lifts the middle of the keyboard slightly and angles the key rows, so your wrists sit more neutral without separating the halves. That is why it needs so little adjustment.

It ranks second because the correction is milder than a true split, and it costs more than the $25 to $50 Perixx. But it beats every split here on transition: if you type all day and cannot afford a week of slow output, the wave is the safer choice. The ProtoArc offers a mouse as well, but a less refined keyboard.

Buy it if you are moving from a flat board. The caveat is ambition: it will not fix severe wrist strain the way a split does.
products.idealFor: Anyone switching from a flat keyboard.

products.name: Arteck Split Ergonomic Keyboard with Palm Rest, 2.4G USB Wireless
products.verdict: A real split with a cushioned rest and no cable.
products.description:
This Arteck is a split, angled keyboard with a built-in cushioned palm rest and a 2.4G USB wireless receiver, in the $50 to $100 bucket. The angled halves bring your hands to a more natural position, and the 2.4G receiver avoids Bluetooth pairing, so it works the moment it is plugged in.

It ranks third as the cheapest wireless split here, though it costs more than the wired Perixx, and the Perixx also uses no receiver or batteries. Against the backlit Arteck below, it gives up the backlight but loses the cable that crowds a desk.

Buy it if you want split ergonomics with a clean desk. The caveat is the receiver: it occupies a USB port and needs power, so the battery life of the board is something to plan around.
products.skipIf: You want a cable free of charging.

products.name: Arteck Split Ergonomic Keyboard with Palm Rest, USB Wired Backlit Keyboard
products.verdict: Split layout with backlit keys for dark rooms.
products.description:
This wired Arteck keeps the split, angled layout and cushioned palm rest, and adds backlit keys, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Backlighting is a practical ergonomic extra for a split: when you are learning a new key layout, being able to see the keys in a dim room reduces typing errors.

It ranks fourth because the cable and the higher price outweigh the backlight for most users when the Perixx offers a split at a lower bucket. It also loses the wireless freedom of the other Arteck. The two share the same split and palm rest, so you are choosing between a light and a cord.

Buy it if you type at night or in dim rooms. The caveat is that a backlit wired board suits a fixed desk, not a laptop bag.
products.skipIf: You never work in low light.

products.name: ProtoArc EKM01 Plus Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard Mouse Combo, Gray Black
products.verdict: Keyboard and mouse together, still under $100.
products.description:
The ProtoArc EKM01 Plus bundles a wireless ergonomic keyboard with a matched mouse, in the $50 to $100 bucket for both devices together. Replacing both at once matters because a poor mouse can undo the posture gains of a good keyboard. The matched design means wrist angles stay consistent.

It ranks fifth because you pay for two devices, so the keyboard alone is less refined than the dedicated Perixx or Wave Keys. The listing offers few keyboard details, such as layout type or palm rest design, which makes it harder to judge against the Arteck splits.

Buy it if you want to replace both devices in one purchase. The caveat is depth: if you already have a mouse you like, a dedicated keyboard gives you more keyboard for the money.

products.name: X9 Wired Ergonomic Keyboard - Comfortable Typing, Ergonomic Full Size
products.verdict: A one-piece curved full-size keyboard at a very low tier.
products.description:
The X9 is a wired full-size keyboard with a one-piece curved ergonomic frame, in the $25 to $50 bucket. A full-size layout keeps the number pad, which accountants and data entry staff rely on, and the curve gently angles the key rows without a split.

It ranks sixth because a single curved piece offers less posture benefit than the Perixx at the same bucket, and it has no wrist rest listed. The RECCAZR below it adds a rest, but the X9 keeps the fuller layout. Both are a plain, low-cost way to start with ergonomics.

Choose it for a basic curved board that stays cheap. The caveat is the mild correction: if you already feel wrist strain, step up to a true split like the Perixx or an Arteck.

products.name: RECCAZR Ergonomic Keyboard, Wired Computer USB Keyboard with Wrist Rest
products.verdict: A curved wired keyboard with an attached wrist rest.
products.description:
The RECCAZR is a wired USB keyboard with a curved ergonomic layout and an attached wrist rest, in the $25 to $50 bucket. The wrist rest is the key spec: it supports the heel of your hand and reduces upward bend, the cheapest ergonomic benefit available.

It ranks last because its curve is gentler than a split and the listing adds little else. The Perixx offers a genuine split and a padded rest at the same bucket, and the X9 offers a full-size curve. This one only leads on the attached rest, which a separate pad could replace.

Buy it for a budget board with wrist support. The caveat is the gentle ergonomics, so skip it if you want stronger posture correction.
products.skipIf: You want a split or wireless design.

whatMatters.detail: A real split has two separate halves, while a curved board is a single bent piece. The split corrects wrist angle more, but takes longer to learn. Look at the product photos and the word split in the title. The Perixx and both Arteck models are true splits, while the X9 and RECCAZR are curved.

A wrist rest reduces the upward bend of your hands while you type. At budget prices it is often missing or too thin. The Perixx has a padded rest, the Wave Keys a cushioned palm rest, and the RECCAZR an attached one. Check the title for wrist rest or palm rest, and note whether it detaches, since a fixed rest is harder to clean and cannot be moved out of the way.

Wired boards avoid batteries and pairing but add a cable. Wireless boards remove the cable but need a receiver or battery. The Arteck wireless uses a 2.4G USB receiver, and the Wave Keys is wireless as well. Check the connection line in the bullets and whether the receiver ships in the box. A dropped receiver can strand a wireless board.

Aggressive layouts take days to adapt to, and your typing speed will fall at first. A gentle wave, like the Logitech Wave Keys, takes far less. Decide how long you can tolerate slower typing, and plan the switch for a lighter week rather than a deadline, and keep your old board nearby for a few days.

A combo includes a mouse, so compare its single price with buying both separately. The ProtoArc is listed under $100 for the pair. Check the price bucket and what ships in the box, and confirm that the mouse suits your hand size before treating it as a bonus, because a mouse that fits badly cancels out the savings.

faq.q: Can I get a real split keyboard under $100?
faq.a: Yes. The Perixx PERIBOARD-512B and both Arteck models are true split designs, and all three sit under $100. The Perixx is the cheapest, at $25 to $50, with a fixed angle, so it suits desks where shoulder width does not need tuning.

faq.q: Will it take long to adjust?
faq.a: A split takes longer than a wave. Expect slower typing for several days. The Logitech Wave Keys lists minimal adjustment, so it suits anyone who cannot afford a productivity drop, such as a writer on deadline.

faq.q: Is the Logitech Wave Keys worth it over the Perixx?
faq.a: If you want wireless and an easier transition, yes. The Wave Keys is a one-piece wave with a cushioned palm rest. If you want a true split for less, the Perixx wins.

faq.q: How do I set up the 2.4G model?
faq.a: Plug the USB receiver into a free port and switch the keyboard on. The wireless Arteck uses a 2.4G receiver, so no Bluetooth pairing is needed. Keep the receiver away from a crowded hub to avoid dropouts, and switch the board off when you leave the desk.

faq.q: How do I clean a keyboard with a wrist rest?
faq.a: Wipe the rest with a slightly damp cloth, then tip the keyboard upside down and shake out crumbs. Do not soak a wrist rest, such as the ones on the Perixx or RECCAZR, since foam can hold moisture and the rest may peel or smell.

It can. The ProtoArc is listed under $100 for both the keyboard and the mouse, which can be cheaper than buying a split keyboard and a separate ergonomic mouse, though the keyboard in the bundle is less refined.

finalTake: Buy the Perixx PERIBOARD-512B for the cheapest genuine split. Choose the Logitech Wave Keys if you want comfort with almost no learning curve, and the wireless Arteck if the cable is the problem. Treat the curved X9 and RECCAZR as entry boards, since a single curve offers milder posture gains than a split.
